description: Kirby Landers is building PoleWindow, a web app that helps pick lunar south pole landing sites. It uses NASA JPL DE421 ephemerides to compute when the Sun (solar power) and Earth (direct-to-Earth comms) are above the horizon at each site, and ranks the sites. Built in Python/Flask from Osorno, Chile. We welcome help with testing, UI, slides and English writing.
summary: PoleWindow is a browser app that helps pick lunar south pole landing sites. Using NASA JPL DE421 ephemerides and LRO LOLA terrain, it computes hour by hour over 2027 when the Sun (solar power) and Earth (direct-to-Earth comms) are above the real terrain horizon. It shows an interactive polar map you can click anywhere, a date-range selector, aligned Sun/Earth/Both timelines, an automatic ranking with continuous-sunlight and Earth-blackout metrics, a LOLA slope check with warnings, distance to permanently shadowed areas, and a simplified launch-window estimate. Key finding: with real terrain, the floors of Shackleton, Haworth and Faustini are in permanent shadow, while Connecting Ridge gets 57% sunlight and 30% Sun and Earth together. Everything is in English and Spanish, runs with no install, and was verified against JPL Horizons.
details:
What it does: PoleWindow answers a core question for south pole missions: at a given site and date range, when will a lander have sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communications? It compares five cited sites (Connecting Ridge and Peak Near Shackleton from Gracy & Lee, LPSC 2024 #1695; Shackleton, Haworth and Faustini crater centers from the IAU/USGS Gazetteer) and any point the user clicks on the polar map between 84°S and the pole.

How it works: Sun and Earth positions are computed with Skyfield using the JPL DE421 ephemeris and NAIF SPICE lunar orientation kernels (MOON_ME frame), hourly for all of 2027 (8,760 samples). The local horizon of every grid point (4,597 points) is derived from LRO LOLA elevation data (LDEM_75S_240M), so crater walls and ridges block the Sun and Earth realistically; a smooth spherical horizon can be toggled for comparison. Slope comes from LOLA LDSM_75S_240M. Results are precomputed into a compact binary file and the static web page recomputes every statistic in the browser for any date range: Sun %, Earth %, Sun+Earth %, longest continuous sunlight, longest night, longest Earth blackout, number of Earth contact drop-outs, slope warnings, distance to permanently shadowed regions, and a simplified launch-window estimate. Geometry was cross-checked against the NASA JPL Horizons API (difference about 0.00001°).

Benefits: mission planners, students and the public can compare sites and dates in seconds, with no install, login or API key, in English or Spanish.

Tools: Python, NumPy, Skyfield, Flask (local version), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, GitHub Pages.

Limitations: 240 m terrain resolution is regional, not landing-scale; the permanent-shadow proxy misses small cold traps; the launch planner ignores vehicle performance and orbit design; official Artemis III region coordinates are not published, so they are not drawn.
dataRefs: NASA JPL DE421 planetary ephemeris (via Skyfield) for Sun, Earth and Moon positions.
NASA NAIF SPICE lunar kernels (moon_080317.tf, pck00008.tpc, moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc), MOON_ME frame.
LRO LOLA LDEM_75S_240M (elevation) and LDSM_75S_240M (slope), PDS Geosciences Node, for the terrain horizon, shaded relief and slope checks.
NASA JPL Horizons System API to validate our Sun/Earth azimuth and elevation.
NASA Artemis III candidate landing region releases (2022 and 2024) for context.
projectRefs: IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: Shackleton 5450, Haworth 14502, Faustini 1919.
NASA news releases on Artemis III candidate regions (Aug 2022, Oct 2024).
